body:
Chapter Seven

To the Dark Portal

The ship that would carry Falanaras south had been an elven destroyer during the Second War, built to hunt Horde vessels beneath skies fouled by dragonfire. Peace had stripped its weapons before the Scourge gave old hulls new purpose. The scars of refitting remained beneath fresh lacquer: sealed firing ports, patched rails, and blue-and-silver wardwork showing through blood-red paint. It had survived one war to carry them toward the remains of another world.

Falanaras stood at the foot of the gangplank with Rynel’s summons inside his coat and a captain’s insignia fastened at his throat. The metal had been straight when Halduron set it there. Lethira had "corrected" it afterward. He had resisted touching it since.

Along the southern quay, sailors loaded crystal cases, weapon racks, field chests, and enough preserved food to make secrecy look like ordinary military caution. Magisters inspected each warded crate before it crossed the plank. Rangers searched spaces already searched by soldiers. No banner named the company, though the prince’s phoenix appeared on every order that mattered.

“Captain Dawnspear?”

He turned too slowly. The quartermaster waiting beside the gangplank noticed. Her expression suggested that grief, inexperience, and damaged hearing were equally inconvenient entries on a manifest.

“Twelve soldiers assigned to your file,” she said. “Six spellbreakers, four conventional infantry, two archers. You berth aft beneath the officers’ deck. Your predecessor’s kit arrived an hour ago.”

“My kit arrived with me.”

“His was in storage.” She offered him a brass key. “The glaive rack is empty.”

The clarification spared neither of them. Falanaras took the key and climbed aboard.

His assigned soldiers waited near the mainmast in traveling armor. Several had served under officers dead in the Ghostlands; he saw it in the disciplined care with which they avoided studying him. He gave them the marching order, the watch rotation, and the location of the emergency mana stores. Rynel’s old sequence came to him without invitation: names first, tasks second, danger reduced until it could be obeyed.

When he finished, a broad-shouldered veteran at the rear saluted. “Sir Daric Sunward. I have the infantry.” A scar crossed his mouth and pulled one corner downward, giving every word a disapproving cast. “Rynel Starweaver trained at the old eastern court.”

“He trained me.”

Daric’s eyes touched the new insignia. “Then we will discover what survived the instruction.”

Falanaras might have resented him if the words had held contempt. They carried only a soldier’s demand for proof. “First watch is yours.”

Daric saluted again. This time, approval moved faintly through it.

The quay bells sounded departure. Lines came free. Beyond the harbor wards, the Forbidding Sea waited under a gray morning, its surface pressed flat by distant rain. Falanaras searched the figures behind the gate until he found Theron’s rigid brace and Lethira’s black-fletched arrow raised between two fingers. Neither had obeyed his request to stay away.

He lifted one hand. Theron answered. Lethira lowered the arrow with exaggerated care, as though concluding a threat.

Silvermoon receded behind masts and red-gold towers. The rebuilt portions caught the weak sun. Farther west, roofs gave way to scaffolds and open sky. Falanaras watched until distance softened the broken quarter, then hated the sea for making ruin look whole.

***

Lady Liadrin came on deck after the harbor disappeared.

Falanaras knew her before any herald spoke the name. The years had changed her clothing first. She wore dark traveling plate beneath a crimson mantle, without the white robes or temple gold that memory insisted upon. Her copper hair was bound high and severe.

The woman crossing the deck carried no staff. No holy symbol hung at her throat. Sailors moved aside for her with the alert respect offered to someone likely to assume command before asking who possessed it.

Grand Magister Rommath followed with two magisters and an escort whose ceremonial polish had failed to conceal field repairs. Rommath’s crimson robes seemed untouched by the damp. His gaze moved over rigging, soldiers, wards, and horizon with the same impatience, finding each insufficient in its own fashion.

The senior magister beside him was Astalor Bloodsworn. Falanaras recognized the name from the sealed manifest and from warding papers copied throughout Silvermoon. Astalor was lean, silver-haired, and attending to the green fire along the gunwale with quiet, unmistakable interest. He held two fingers a breath above it as he walked, reading each change in the flame without disturbing the boundary.

Magister Selorien Dawnmark followed half a step behind with a slate tucked against his forearm. He had the drawn face of a man accustomed to confirming difficult conclusions and turning them into procedures a crew could repeat. “Master Bloodsworn, the ship's artificer asked to be warned before we assessed his boundary.”

“Then he should be informed,” Astalor said. The fire dipped at a stanchion. “There is a nine-percent loss here. The repair beneath it is conducting unevenly. Please ask him to join us when he is free.”

Selorien marked the slate. “I will find him before breakfast becomes a formal grievance.” Astalor's mouth softened at one corner. “Bring the repair record as well. If his work has lasted this long under an uneven load, I would like to know how.” Selorien added a second note. “A grievance and a compliment. He may forgive the inspection.”

Liadrin stopped before Falanaras. Her eyes went to his insignia and remained there long enough to acknowledge its freshness.

“Captain Dawnspear,” she said. “You carry Starweaver’s summons.”

“I do.”

“And his command?”

“What remains of it.”

Her attention sharpened. Falanaras expected correction. Instead she said, “Remnants are the greater part of Quel’Thalas now. We have become skilled at making them serve.”

Rommath glanced back. “Lady Liadrin.”

“The deck will remain under us for another moment, Grand Magister.” Her eyes stayed on Falanaras. “Have we met?”

“At the inner gate during the fall. I was wounded. You asked if I could hold a weapon.”

Liadrin studied his face. “What did you answer?”

“Yes.”

“I remember the answer. Half the wounded lied to me that day.” Her voice held no warmth, yet neither did it diminish the memory. “Some lies are a bridge across one necessary hour.”

She turned to join Rommath. Falanaras watched her go, the remembered priestess receding beneath dark plate and a crimson mantle.

Every soldier in Silvermoon had heard what became of the high priestess after the Sunwell fell. Liadrin no longer served the Light she had once carried among the wounded, and she made no secret of believing that it had abandoned their people.

Some repeated the story with grief, others with approval, and a few with the avid certainty of people relieved to see sacred things fail someone more important than themselves.

Falanaras had never doubted the reports. The dark plate, the empty place at her throat, and the way Rommath addressed her as a military equal left nothing to explain.

What unsettled him was the memory of her certainty at the inner gate. She had believed completely while the kingdom died around her. Whatever had replaced that faith had been built from the same severity.

He watched her join Rommath without calling her back. To ask why she had turned from the Light would have been to ask what the fall had cost her, as though Silvermoon did not carry the answer in every ruined street.

When the breakfast bell rang, he realized his bandaged hands had begun to ache where no scars remained.

***

The voyage taught rank to surrender before weather.

By the second morning, three magisters had been sick over the lee rail, two soldiers had bruises from misjudging ladders, and Sir Daric had acquired the permanent stance of a man fighting the deck. Captain Althene Starwind, who commanded the ranger file, moved with insulting ease. She was spare, sharp-featured, and old enough to remember seas before most of the sailors had been born.

“Your infantryman is trying to threaten the horizon into stillness,” she told Falanaras.

Daric’s face had gone the color of old wax. “It has shown poor discipline.”

“Should I confine it?” Falanaras asked.

Daric considered the water. “At the first opportunity.”

The exchange earned a brief sound from Althene, too dry for laughter. It was the first time anyone in Falanaras’s file had spoken around him without weighing the dead captain between each word.

By the second afternoon, Eversong's gold had fallen behind them. West of the ship, forested ridges rose toward Zul'Aman, their upper slopes hidden by cloud. Amani watchfires marked two heights even in daylight. No boats came out, but every ranger on deck watched the shore until the last smoke vanished astern.

South of the Amani country, the coast bore the same sickness as the Ghostlands without any surviving ward to hold it back. Bare woods reached down to black shingle. A ruined pier leaned into yellow water beneath the Eastern Plaguelands, and carrion birds rose from it in a single dark cloud as the ship passed. The crew kept well offshore and drew drinking water only from sealed casks.

Routine took hold. At dawn the soldiers drilled in pairs wherever the deck allowed. Rangers checked the coast from the foremast. The magisters fed power into the ship’s boundary at noon and dusk, maintaining a thin distortion that made distant observers see an unremarkable trader riding low in the water. Falanaras inspected weapons, heard reports, and learned which of his soldiers hid shaking hands by volunteering for rope work.

The ship’s mana allotment was measured twice daily. Crystal dust went into watered wine for the common file. Officers received small cut stones and the expectation that they would need less supervision. The first evening, Falanaras found one of his spellbreakers standing too close to the engine housing, breathing in time with its pulse.

He gave the soldier his own ration and reassigned him beside Daric until the glassy focus left his eyes. No accusation passed between them. By supper, the matter had become a change in watch rotation and nothing more.

“You report him?” Althene asked later.

They stood by the stern while the coast slid past beneath cloud. Forested heights rose to the west, dark with distance. Sea birds followed the wake and fought over refuse from the galley.

“He took the ration and returned to duty,” Falanaras said.

“That was not my question.”

“No.”

Althene nodded toward the engine housing. “Rangers distrust dependence because we spend too much time beyond easy supply. Magisters call that superstition. Soldiers call it a problem when someone misses formation. Everyone becomes wise after the failure.”

Rynel’s overbright eyes rose in Falanaras’s memory. “Then wisdom is late.”

“Usually.” Althene rested her forearms on the rail. “You gave him your ration. Eat near a ward tonight. Quietly. If you fall over tomorrow, I will report both of you for making concern inefficient.”

He did as instructed. The nearest ward burned beside the chart room, where Rommath and Astalor spent their evenings behind a locked door. Falanaras sat outside with his back against the bulkhead and felt the green current ease the pressure behind his teeth.

Voices carried through the boards.

“The prince asked for capacity,” Rommath said. “He did not ask for a survey of every neglected mechanism between Silvermoon and the Portal.”

“Capacity without failure tolerances tells us very little,” Astalor replied. “Our readings show that the aft boundary is losing more power than its instruments report. We should understand the discrepancy before it chooses the occasion for us.”

Selorien's answer came lower. “I repeated the measurements from the engine relay. They support Master Bloodsworn's finding. I have given the captain a repair sequence that will hold until landfall without requiring him to dismantle the stern.”

The latch opened. Falanaras stood, expecting reprimand. Rommath looked from him to the ward and understood at once.

“If you require power, Captain, request it,” the Grand Magister said. “Starving discreetly remains starvation. It gains no virtue from manners.”

He passed Falanaras a crystal from his sleeve and continued toward the officers’ stair. The stone held more energy than two standard rations. Rommath had offered it as casually as a commander correcting an uneven strap.

Astalor paused in the doorway. His gaze settled on the crystal. “That is a generous dose for you, Captain. If you are willing, note when the relief begins to recede. It would help us set the next allotment more accurately.”

Selorien shifted the slate beneath his arm. “I can add the observation to the ration record. The captain has enough reports of his own.”

“A sensible division,” Astalor said. He looked at Falanaras rather than through him. “One observation will suffice. We are trying to make the allotment fit the soldier rather than the reverse.”

“I will,” Falanaras said.

Selorien tapped the slate. “At last, a measurement the quartermaster may thank us for.”

“Then it will be rarer than the crystal,” Astalor said, with the faintest smile.

“I will leave space in the record,” Selorien said, following him toward the stair.

On the third day, the plague-gray shore gave way to the Hinterlands. Forest climbed from the water in dark ranks, broken by pale cliffs and narrow falls that vanished into spray before reaching the sea. Once, three gryphons wheeled above a headland watchtower. Althene tracked them until distance took them behind the trees.

The coast bent west and returned in broad, hazy reaches. River water stained the sea brown around them, carrying branches, reeds, and once the swollen body of a horse. By evening the wind had begun to sharpen from the east, and the sailors reefed sail while the shore disappeared behind advancing rain.

***

The storm reached them on the fourth night.

Wind struck from the east and drove the ship toward a coast hidden by rain. The first squall tore a foresail before the sailors could reef it. Canvas cracked overhead. A loose line swept the deck and caught one soldier across the legs, flinging him against the rail.

Falanaras reached him before the next roll. He hooked one arm through the rail and caught the soldier’s harness with the other. Daric seized Falanaras at the waist while Althene cut the thrashing line. Salt water crossed the deck hard enough to blind them all.

“Boundary is failing!” a sailor shouted.

Green fire along the gunwale broke into scattered tongues. The disguise collapsed with it. For a moment the ship showed itself upon the open sea in full military aspect, crystal lamps blazing and crimson armor crowded along the deck.

Rommath emerged without a cloak. Rain flattened his hair and ran over his face. He lifted both hands, caught the broken ward-lines above the mast, and drew them together until fire stretched between his fingers.

“Astalor, aft focus. Selorien, keep the engine from compensating.” His voice carried through the gale. “Liadrin, clear the mast.”

Liadrin was already moving. She climbed into the forward rigging with a sailor’s knife between her teeth, plate abandoned somewhere below. Two deckhands followed until a spar broke loose above them. Liadrin braced one boot against the mast, caught the spar’s line, and took its full weight across her harness while the sailors crawled past.

There was no gold around her. No prayer reached Falanaras through the rain. She held because people were beneath her and released only when they were clear.

Astalor knelt at the shattered aft focus with one palm suspended inside exposed ward-fire and the other marking the current's pulse against the deck. Selorien worked at the engine relay under his direction, calling back each measurement and checking it against the relay's response. Green light climbed Astalor's wrist in controlled bands. He watched it with intent fascination, adjusting the angle of his hand whenever the current tried to close around him. His calm suggested mastery remained a reasonable expectation even while it burned him.

“Feedback is rising past the second limit,” Selorien shouted.

“I have it,” Astalor called. “On my third count, break the compensator. We can return the release to the boundary. One. Two. Three.”

Selorien struck the compensator with the iron cap of his staff. The crystal split exactly as Astalor tore his hand free. The released current flashed across the deck and vanished into the restored boundary. Astalor caught the rail, steadied himself, and looked first to the ward above them rather than the burn climbing his palm.

“The boundary was three breaths from failure,” Astalor said through the storm. “Record the interval. Reduce the aft draw by one twentieth, and next time we will keep the operator outside the current.”

Selorien made the adjustment, then caught Astalor's burned hand and wrapped it without ceremony. “I will make that the first step in the revised sequence.” Astalor surrendered the hand without protest. The finding was his; Selorien was already turning it into a procedure another magister could survive.

Falanaras secured the injured soldier beneath the quarterdeck, then returned to the mast with Daric and four others. They hauled the torn sail down hand over hand. The wind pulled blood from their palms through wet gloves. When a soldier lost his footing, Daric took the rope across his own shoulder and roared until the man found the deck again.

The ward closed at last. The ship faded beneath rain and bent light. Westward, two pale lamps had appeared on the hidden shore. They remained fixed upon the sea for several minutes, searching, then turned inland.

“Observers?” Falanaras asked Althene.

She wiped rain from her eyes. “Humans, perhaps. Dwarves if we have offended good fortune. Whoever they serve, they saw enough to invent the rest.”

Rommath descended from the quarterdeck. Power still ran between his fingers in thin green threads. “Let them invent. Fear is often more useful than accurate numbers.”

Liadrin dropped from the rigging. Rope had burned a red line across one palm. She wrapped it herself and looked over the deck until every injured sailor had been accounted for.

Falanaras held out a clean strip of linen. “You left command to climb the mast.”

Liadrin took the linen and wound it over the first bandage. “Command remained on deck. The spar did not.”

“Another sailor could have taken the line.”

“Another sailor did. So did I.” She tightened the cloth with her teeth. “Ranks are useful while they put the right hands where they are needed. They become vanity when they excuse those hands from the work.”

Falanaras thought of Rynel bent over the anchor, taking what the escape required and spending it on the passage rather than his own hunger. “And when command fails?”

Liadrin flexed her wrapped hand. “Then people choose what the failure will cost.”

***

After the storm, they reached the waters below the Hinterlands and resumed their long passage down the continent's eastern edge.

The Arathi coast opened beyond a wide river mouth. Tawny slopes showed between bands of rain, crossed by old roads and walls too distant for Falanaras to judge as occupied or ruined. Fishing boats fled toward shore when the disguised destroyer approached, their crews seeing only a trader riding low and refusing to test the appearance.

Falanaras had spent years thinking of the world outside Quel'Thalas as forces pressing against its borders: Scourge from the south, human judgment beyond the mountains, absent allies, returning exiles. From the sea, those forces resolved into grazing land, woodsmoke, roads, and people hauling nets beneath banners he had been taught to resent.

Althene found him watching an Arathi harbor recede at dusk. “Disappointed?”

“By what?”

“That the wider world has ordinary laundry.” She indicated pale cloth strung between houses beyond the seawall. “It weakens the grandeur of foreign enemies.”

“They may wash it with sinister intent.”

“Keep that thought. You are learning command.”

Farther south, the coast grew harsher. In the Twilight Highlands, dark cliffs shouldered into the sea and storm clouds snagged on mountains beyond them. For two evenings a bruise of smoke rested inland above the country of the Badlands and Burning Steppes. Then the shore softened again, and red stone rose among the wooded slopes of Redridge, startlingly bright after the northern gray.

Late in the second week, the red heights sank behind reed-choked river mouths. The air grew warm and heavy. Marsh haze erased the horizon, insects struck the sails far from land, and the water darkened with silt from the Swamp of Sorrows. After midnight the crew altered course and followed a sequence of lights visible only through a magister's lens.

They landed at dawn in a reed-screened inlet where blackwater streams met the sea. Blood elf engineers held a narrow strip of firm ground behind layered concealments, with three low storehouses, a timber jetty, and a ward tower disguised as a dead cypress. Every face on the quay had the weathered, sleepless look of service far from Silvermoon.

They unloaded before the sun cleared the trees. No welcoming party waited and no local ruler claimed a toll. By midmorning the retinue had formed around carts, pack animals, and warded cases, then turned west through the Swamp of Sorrows toward the Blasted Lands.

***

Beyond the marsh, the land had been burned too deeply to recover.

Red earth broke beneath their boots. Thorn trees clung to gullies with roots exposed, and hot wind carried grit into armor joints, mouths, and water skins. The sky looked bleached near the horizon. Even the carrion birds circled without calling.

Falanaras had known dead places. The Ghostlands crawled with corrupted magic and the old pressure of the Sunwell’s wound. The Blasted Lands offered an emptier hostility. Power did not pulse beneath the soil. It had passed through and left the ground exhausted.

By the second day inland, everyone felt it. Conversations shortened. Soldiers watched the warded carts too often. One magister snapped at a pack animal and spent the next hour apologizing to no one. Rommath ordered the mana ration increased before any officer requested it.

“This is temporary,” he told the assembled captains. “Do not confuse endurance with deprivation. We brought sufficient stores, and stores serve no purpose unopened.”

Daric drank his portion and rolled his shoulders as relief reached them. “The Grand Magister makes indulgence sound punitive.”

“It improves compliance,” Selorien said. As Astalor's assistant, he was checking the emptied vials against the official allotment and a second record of field observations, repeating any comparison that failed to agree. “Pleasure invites debate.”

Astalor held his own vial toward the sun, studying the residue. “Please keep the local absence separate from our shipboard readings. The contrast should let us distinguish adaptation from ration decay. A miserable environment has given us unusually useful conditions.”

“After we reach the Portal,” Rommath said. “Until then, measure whether the column remains fit to reach it.”

Astalor inclined his head. “Of course. The column comes first. We will reserve the adaptation study until after we reach the Portal.” Selorien moved to the next entry, carrying the priority through both ledgers.

Their route turned through a ravine where old siege damage had fused stones together in black ridges. Althene halted the column at its mouth. Three figures watched from the heights, wrapped against the dust.

“Scouts,” she said. “Human equipment. They have been with us since noon.”

Daric rested a hand on his sword. “Do we remove them?”

“If they wished to challenge the route, they would bring more than three,” Rommath said. “They want numbers, names, and confidence. Deny the last two.”

The retinue entered the ravine without changing pace. Falanaras felt the observers’ attention follow the crimson mantles, green eyes, warded cases, and weapons. Outside Quel’Thalas, their survival had become evidence against them before anyone spoke.

Liadrin walked beside him after they cleared the heights. She had exchanged armor for a lighter coat, though the sword at her side remained within easy reach.

“You disliked being watched,” she said.

“They saw taint before they saw soldiers.”

“Perhaps. We saw enemies before we saw three tired men on a ridge.”

Falanaras glanced at her. “Should we be charitable?”

“We should be exact. Charity is often an excuse for seeing poorly.” She stepped over a split in the road. “They may despise us. They may also be correct that we are dangerous.”

“Does that matter?”

“Everything true matters. It need not decide us.”

Ahead, a cart wheel struck loose stone and broke at the hub. The warded case above it lurched toward the ditch. Daric and three soldiers caught the frame. Green light leaked through the case seams, and every blood elf within sight turned toward it at once.

The moment lasted less than a breath. It was still long enough for shame to pass through the column.

Liadrin walked to the damaged cart and placed both hands beneath the axle. “Lift,” she ordered.

They lifted. Soldiers braced the case. Magisters resealed the seam. No one named the way hunger had moved through them. Work gave the column somewhere else to put its hands.

When the new wheel was fixed, Liadrin looked down the line. “We continue.”

Falanaras heard more in the two words than movement. The prince had gone ahead through prisons, hostile kingdoms, and harsher roads, then sent back power, instruction, and summons. Silvermoon had made a creed from following because the alternative was to remain among its graves.

He touched the message case beneath his coat. Rynel had died to send another officer onward. Falanaras could honor the choice without pretending the road had chosen him kindly.

***

They saw the Dark Portal before sunset on the fourth day of the march.

At first it seemed another ridge standing above the red plain. Then distance yielded the pillars, vast and dark against the western sky, and the stone figures crouched upon them with their faces turned toward the road. Green radiance filled the arch between. It did not flicker like fire. It revolved slowly, depth opening where no depth should exist.

The column lost its conversations one by one.

Falanaras had expected a gate. Gates belonged to walls, roads, and hands that could close them. This stood alone amid the ruin it had caused, large enough to make armies look temporary.

Blood elf fortifications ringed the approach. Low barricades, ward pylons, and canvas shelters occupied ground scarred by older camps. Engineers moved among humming conduits that ran toward the Portal’s base. Their apparatus did not create the opening; it steadied what greater power had forced from the far side.

Beyond bow range, other watchers kept their own posts on the heights. Human standards showed in the late light. No one approached. Suspicion had arranged itself around the gateway and learned to live there.

A commander from the Portal garrison met Rommath beneath the first pylon. His armor bore Outland dust in pale streaks. He saluted the Grand Magister, Liadrin, and Astalor before turning to the captains.

“Transit is stable,” he said. “The receiving station reports clear ground. Cross in ordered files, no pauses within the threshold. Keep eyes forward if vertigo takes you. If you hear voices behind you, they are carried resonance.”

Daric leaned toward Falanaras. “I preferred the sea.”

“You threatened it with confinement.”

“It improved afterward, didn’t it?”

Camp formed for one final night on Azeroth. Soldiers ate beside the ward pylons. Rangers inspected the road behind them as though Quel’Thalas might appear at its end. Astalor spent an hour questioning the engineers, listening as closely to their descriptions of the Portal's behavior as to the instrument readings. Selorien laid each answer beside the logs and marked the points that required a repeatable procedure. When the account was complete, Astalor thanked the engineers and sent them to supper. Selorien remained with him to reduce their findings to a sequence the next watch could use.

Falanaras could not sleep. The Portal’s hum entered the ground and rose through his bedroll. Near midnight he walked beyond the tents and found Liadrin standing at the edge of the lit approach.

Green light moved across her face. For an instant it recalled the radiance beneath Silvermoon’s gate, altered in color and stripped of mercy.

“Do you know what the prince wants?” he asked.

“Enough.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the portion you require tonight.” She looked toward the turning radiance. “Tomorrow you will see a world where our prince found allies after humans imprisoned him, where our people learned methods Silvermoon now depends upon, and where survival has demanded more than it demanded at home. Decide nothing in advance. Watch what each necessity asks of the person naming it.”

“And if I decide the cost is too high?”

Liadrin’s gaze settled on the insignia at his throat. “Then know what you would let die instead.”

She returned to camp. Falanaras remained before the Portal until the cold drove through his coat. The answer troubled him because Rynel had already given it another form. At the anchor, the captain had chosen what his failure would cost and who would live instead.

Dawn came red through the dust.

The retinue formed in marching order. Rommath crossed first with the garrison commander. Astalor waited beside the threshold until the engineers confirmed that the ward pylons had settled. He compared their count with his own instruments, thanked them, and entered at the prescribed interval. Selorien followed at his shoulder, carrying one case while Astalor carried the other. Liadrin entered alone, shoulders square beneath her crimson mantle. Green swallowed each of them without ripple or sound.

Captain Althene led the rangers. Daric took the infantry file. Falanaras stood at the head of the spellbreakers with Rynel’s summons against his heart.

Behind him lay the sea road, Silvermoon, Theron’s brace, Lethira’s raised arrow, Halduron’s rebuke, and a gatehouse collapsed over the man whose place he carried. Ahead waited Kael’thas and the answer for which Quel’Thalas had spent so much hope.

The Portal filled his sight. Its power pressed against every hungry part of him, immense and unreachable. Within the green, a second sky burned red.

Falanaras gave the order to advance and stepped out of Azeroth.
synopsis: Promoted in the aftermath of Deatholme, Falanaras joins the blood elf retinue answering Kael’thas’s summons alongside Lady Liadrin, senior magister Astalor Bloodsworn, his assistant Selorien Dawnmark, Grand Magister Rommath, and other soldiers and rangers. They sail aboard a refitted Thalassian destroyer left from the Second War. Falanaras recognizes Liadrin as the high priestess he glimpsed during Quel’Thalas’s fall, but he already knows her faith ended when she judged that the Light had abandoned their people; what unsettles him is the severity that survived its loss. Shipboard hunger, routine, and a violent storm reveal the retinue through action, including Astalor’s controlled technical command and Selorien’s practical support. The voyage follows the eastern coast past Zul’Aman, the plague-marked northern lands, the Hinterlands, Arathi, the southern highlands, and Redridge before the company lands covertly in the Swamp of Sorrows. They march west through the Blasted Lands, reach the blood-elf-held Dark Portal route, and cross into Outland.
title: Chapter 7: To the Dark Portal
